beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson three. Floating ice, and water the solvent. [[ice]]Ice floats, and that quietly protects life in every lake. [[salt]]And water dissolves salt, sugar, and the proteins inside you. [[count]]Then we will count how much is dissolved, using moles and molarity.
beats.ice: Start with ice. [[liquid]]In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form all the time, so the molecules tumble close together. [[freeze]]As the water freezes, the bonds stop breaking. [[lock]]Each molecule is held by four bonds, at fixed angles, and together they build an open lattice with gaps in it. [[space]]Locked apart like this, the same molecules take up more room. [[dense]]More room for the same mass means a lower density. So ice is less dense than liquid water, and it floats.
beats.lake: Why does this matter? Think of a lake in winter. [[cool]]As water cools, it gets denser, until about four degrees Celsius, where it is at its densest. [[sink]]Colder water, just above freezing, begins to lock into the lattice, so it expands and stays near the top. [[lid]]At the surface it freezes, and the ice floats as a lid. [[below]]That lid slows the heat leaving the water below, so the lake stays liquid underneath, and the fish survive. [[sinkice]]If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, and could freeze solid.
beats.q1: Quick check. Why does ice float?
beats.solv: Now, water as a solvent. [[mix]]A solution is a mixture that is the same all the way through. [[solvent]]The substance doing the dissolving is the solvent. [[solute]]The substance that is dissolved is the solute. [[aq]]When the solvent is water, it is an aqueous solution. [[why]]Water is a good solvent because its molecules are polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end and slightly positive hydrogen ends, and because they form hydrogen bonds so readily.
beats.hydr: Take table salt, sodium chloride. [[crystal]]In the crystal, small positive sodium ions and larger negative chloride ions are packed together. [[water]]Water molecules crowd around its surface. [[na]]Around a sodium ion, the negative oxygen ends point in. [[cl]]Around a chloride ion, the positive hydrogen ends point in. [[pull]]Each ion is pulled out of the crystal, and water closes around it. [[shell]]That sphere of water molecules is a hydration shell. [[done]]Wrapped like this, the ions stay apart, and the salt is dissolved. [[limit]]There is a limit, though. Only about thirty-six grams of salt will dissolve in a hundred milliliters of water at room temperature.
beats.phil: Water dissolves more than ions. [[polar]]Polar molecules, like sugar, have charged patches that water bonds to. [[protein]]A large molecule such as a protein dissolves too, if it has ionic and polar regions on its surface. [[phil]]A substance with an affinity for water is called hydrophilic. [[oil]]Oil is different. Its molecules have no charged or polar regions, so water has nothing to hold on to. [[phobic]]Such a substance is hydrophobic. The water bonds to itself instead, and pushes the oil into drops.
beats.conc: Most reactions in cells happen in water. [[collide]]And a reaction needs molecules to collide. [[more]]The more solute in each liter, the more often they meet. [[count]]So we need a way to say how much is dissolved.
beats.mole: First, a way to count. [[mass]]Molecular mass is the sum of the masses of all the atoms in a molecule. Water has two hydrogens, at one each, and an oxygen at sixteen, so eighteen. [[mol]]Molecules are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count in moles. [[avo]]One mole is six point zero two times ten to the twenty-third units, whether atoms, molecules, or ions. That is Avogadro's number. [[molar]]The mass of one mole is the molar mass, in grams per mole. It is the same number as the molecular mass. So one mole of water is eighteen grams. [[dalton]]One molecule weighs eighteen daltons. The numbers match, but the units are different.
beats.calc: Now for salt. [[nacl]]Sodium is twenty-three, and chlorine is thirty-five and a half. So the molar mass of sodium chloride is fifty-eight and a half grams per mole. [[formula]]The number of moles is the mass, divided by the molar mass. [[ex]]Take eleven point seven grams of salt. Eleven point seven divided by fifty-eight and a half is point two moles.
beats.molar: Now we can state a concentration. [[def]]Molarity is the moles of solute, per liter of solution. Its unit is M, or moles per liter. [[flask]]Put those eleven point seven grams in a flask, dissolve them, and then add water up to the two hundred fifty milliliter mark. [[sum]]We say the salt is made up to a quarter liter of solution. [[div]]Point two moles, divided by point two five liters, is point eight moles per liter. [[why]]Notice that we divide by the volume of the solution, not by the water we added, because the dissolved salt takes up some of the volume too. [[one]]And fifty-eight and a half grams of salt, made up to one liter, is exactly one molar.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice, so it is less dense and floats, and lakes stay liquid below. [[w2]]Water is the solvent. It dissolves ions in hydration shells, and polar and charged molecules too. Oil is hydrophobic. [[w3]]Moles count molecules, and molar mass links grams to moles. [[w4]]Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
